findings.summary: The caption is copied from Part 1: it promises ten pages and Part 1's topic list, but this part has four pages covering different material.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of BASH QUOTING & EXPANSION. ... 10 pages of field notes on quoting rules, the expansion pipeline, IFS, globbing, parameter expansion, arrays, and \"$@\" vs $*." — the part contains 4 slides: Forwarding Arguments; Where Missing Quotes Bite; eval, Backticks, and The Seven Rules; Debugging, Preamble, and Tools.
findings.fix: Rewrite the caption for this part: "4 pages on forwarding arguments with \"$@\", where missing quotes bite, eval and backticks, the seven rules, and the debugging preamble."

findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual hook in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of BASH QUOTING & EXPANSION. Every Bash script that breaks on a filename with a space breaks for the same reason: ..."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and move the part label later or into the series field: "Every Bash script that breaks on a filename with a space breaks for the same reason: the shell expands, then splits, then globs, then strips quotes — and an unquoted variable opts into all of it. Part 2 of BASH QUOTING & EXPANSION: 10 pages of field notes ..."

findings.summary: `ssh host "${cmd@Q}"` is a broken idiom: `@Q` on a whole command string makes the remote shell see a single word, not a command line.
findings.fix: With `cmd='ls /tmp'` this sends the literal `'ls /tmp'` and the remote reports `ls /tmp: command not found`. Use `@Q` only on interpolated arguments — `ssh host "grep -r ${pat@Q} /var/log"` — or build the command as an array and send `ssh host "${cmd[*]@Q}"`.

findings.summary: The claim that `set -e` does not fire in an assignment's command substitution is false for a plain assignment, and contradicts the book's own `export` example on page 2.
findings.evidence: "`set -e` does not fire in an assignment's command substitution." — contrasted with page 2's `export VAR=$(cmd)     # masks cmd's exit status`
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "`set -e` DOES fire on `VAR=$(cmd)` — the assignment takes the substitution's status. It is the builtin prefix (`local`/`declare`/`export`/`readonly`) that masks it. What `set -e` ignores without `shopt -s inherit_errexit` is a failing command *inside* the substitution, e.g. `x=$(false; echo hi)`."

findings.summary: The page opens with a bullet block describing the script preamble, but the preamble it refers to is not shown until four blocks later.
findings.evidence: Page 4's first block is `["Worth memorising as a unit.","`set -e` still has the holes from the gotchas page.","Treat it as a helper, not a safety net."]`, while the `"Preamble"` heading and `set -euo pipefail` / `IFS=$'\n\t'` code block appear after the debugging code, the `declare -p` bullets and the Closing Summary callout.
findings.fix: Move that three-item bullet block to directly after the `Preamble` heading and its code block, and give the debugging material that now opens the page its own heading (e.g. "Debug Harness") so the `printf '<%s>\n' "$@"` / `declare -p var` code has a labelled section.

findings.summary: The "Closing Summary" takeaway is placed mid-page, before three further sections of new material (Preamble, Tools, Portability).
findings.evidence: `{"type":"callout","style":"takeaway","title":"Closing Summary","text":"The shell expands, then splits, then globs, then strips quotes..."}` appears immediately before `{"type":"heading","text":"Preamble"}`, `"Tools"` and `"Portability"`.
findings.fix: Move the Closing Summary callout to the end of the page, immediately before the `Leave With This` tip, so the summary follows the last of the new material rather than interrupting it.

findings.summary: `set --` is attributed to the `getopts` builtin, but it belongs to the external `getopt(1)`; the standard step after a `getopts` loop is `shift $((OPTIND-1))`.
findings.evidence: "`set --` is the standard re-parse trick after `getopts`."
findings.fix: Either "`shift $((OPTIND-1))` is the standard step after a `getopts` loop" or "`eval set -- \"$(getopt ...)\"` is the re-parse trick for the external `getopt(1)`" — but not the two conflated.

findings.summary: A red annotation fragment under the "When is "$*" the right choice?" heading is rendered at a tiny size and is illegible.
findings.evidence: Directly below the heading "When is "$*" the right choice?" at the left margin sits an underlined red mark roughly 5-6 px tall (about one third of the 18 px body text) that resolves to something like "Ans—"; no other heading on pages 1-4 carries such a mark.
findings.fix: Render that annotation at the same type size as the surrounding body text, or drop the stray annotation node from the page model if it is not intended content.

findings.summary: In the "Filenames Are Hostile" flowchart, connector arrows cross over node boxes so edges and boxes overlap.
findings.evidence: Between the "forbidden", "newlines" and "quotes, globs" nodes the connector lines run across the box borders instead of terminating at them — the arrow heading toward "quotes, globs" passes over its left border, and "newlines" is entered by two lines from different directions.
findings.fix: Increase the flowchart's node spacing / re-run the layout so edges route between boxes and terminate on their borders rather than crossing them.

findings.summary: The ssh remote-quoting line is filed under a "Status Traps" heading although it is a quoting/re-parsing hazard, not an exit-status one.
findings.evidence: Under `{"type":"heading","text":"Status Traps"}` the first code line is `ssh host "${cmd@Q}"   # remote side re-parses`, followed by the two actual status lines `export VAR=$(cmd)     # masks cmd's exit status` and `VAR=$(cmd) || exit    # split, then export`.
findings.fix: Move the `ssh host "${cmd@Q}"` line into the preceding "Substitution Damage" section (or give it its own "Crossing Into Another Shell" heading) and leave "Status Traps" with only the two `export`/exit-status lines.

findings.summary: Calling array subscripts a quote-free numeric context is false for associative arrays, where an unquoted subscript silently matches the `@`/`*` special keys.
findings.evidence: "Numeric contexts are the one quote-free zone: `$(( ))` and subscripts."
findings.fix: With `declare -A a; a[x]=1; a[y]=2; k='*'`, `${a[$k]}` expands to `1 2` (all values) instead of looking up the key `*`; `${a["$k"]}` is correct. Narrow the claim to "`$(( ))` and *indexed*-array subscripts — associative subscripts are strings and must be quoted."

findings.summary: `printf %q` is introduced as "the other" safe quoting route without this part ever naming the first one it is being contrasted with.
findings.evidence: Page 3 bullet: "`printf %q` is the other safe quoting route." The only prior mention of the alternative is the bare code line `ssh host "${cmd@Q}"   # remote side re-parses` on page 2, and the `eval` bullets on page 3 never name `${var@Q}` as the mitigation.
findings.fix: Rewrite the eval bullets to name the mitigation explicitly — e.g. "If you must build a command string, quote it with `${var@Q}`" — and then change the following bullet to "`printf %q` is the other route to the same result."

findings.summary: The version claim about xtrace quoting is wrong — Bash quoted trace words containing shell metacharacters long before 4.4.
findings.evidence: "`set -x` traces after expansion; Bash 4.4+ quotes the trace."
findings.fix: Bash's `xtrace_print_word_list` has single-quoted words containing shell metacharacters since the 3.x line; the bash-4.4 CHANGES entry is only a bug fix ("commands printed due to `set -x' could be incorrectly quoted if being printed in contexts where they haven't yet been expanded"). Drop the version gate: "`set -x` traces after expansion and single-quotes words that need it."
